title: Primitive Skateboarding Founder Paul Rodriguez on Building a Brand That Outlasts You
summary: How pro skater P-Rod built Primitive into a $20M empire using the fearless mindset he learned from skateboarding.
body_markdown:
Paul Rodriguez has eight X Games medals, 10 signature Nike shoes, and a skateboarding career that’s lasted nearly three decades—far longer than most pros ever get. He also built[Primitive](https://primitiveskate.com/) , the Nike-exclusive sneaker shop that grew into a full skate and apparel brand now making $20 million a year. The thread connecting both is a mindset he learned on a board, built for fear, uncertainty, and risk—the same forces that make running a business feel overwhelming.


Rodriguez is honest that none of it came naturally. He was a kid afraid of the dark who taught himself to get comfortable being uncomfortable, one trick at a time. Here, he breaks down how that mental game transfers to business: why low stakes can be freeing, why focusing on the disaster helps create it, and how a spray-paint accident became a two-minute sellout.


### On why low stakes gave him more freedom, not less:


When we opened the shop, I was 19, freshly living my dream, and honestly, the stakes felt low. People think entrepreneurship has to feel high-stakes—like that pressure is what creates the urgency to succeed. For me it was almost the opposite. I was already doing the thing I loved. If the store didn’t work out, it was all good. Something else would.


There’s a magic in that, and I’ve found it in a few areas of life. When you’re kind of nonchalant about something—like, if it’s meant to happen, it’s meant to happen, and if not, not—things tend to fall into place. My partners were working on the business plan. It’s ready? Cool, we’ll present it, and we’ll leave it in God’s hands. I just stayed focused on my part, which was to skate and keep my name out there.


### On becoming comfortable being uncomfortable through skating:


People assume skaters are just naturally laid-back daredevils. Not me. As a kid I was a worrier. I was afraid of the dark until I was 12, maybe older, and afraid of roller coasters. I’m not a daredevil at all.


But I fell so in love with skating that I got used to being in scary circumstances, and it built a tolerance little by little over time. For me it wasn’t natural—skating instilled it in me. When you’ve been doing something dangerous long enough, you’re constantly facing your fears, the adrenaline, the chance of getting hurt every single day. You kind of live in that space.


So when a situation comes up in business or anywhere else, you’re just comfortable being uncomfortable. You don’t stress it until it actually happens.


Paul “P-Rod” Rodriguez launched (left) Primitive in 2008 as a Nike-exclusive sneaker shop in the San Fernando Valley. *Primitive Skateboarding*


### On why focusing on the disaster helps create the disaster:


This is where you learn to put your focus. You focus on what gives you the best chance of success, not on the disaster—because if you focus on the disaster, you’re gonna help create the disaster. And the disaster doesn’t need any help happening. It’ll take care of itself.


When I’m skating, I’m not thinking, “Don’t fall, don’t fall, don’t fall.” I’m thinking, “Put your foot right here. Go the right speed. Pop exactly at this point.” Your focus is captivated by each little step you have to do.


The truth is, even when you focus only on success, it can still become a disaster. So you have to really, really help the success happen. It almost never happens by accident. Focus on the success, not the disaster.


### On breaking a long-term vision into small wins you can actually feel:


I’ve always had a big long-term vision. You know the goal is there. But you can’t sit and stare at that long-term goal every day, because then everything in between you and it starts seeming overwhelming. You’re like, “I gotta do this and this and this—I’m never gonna get there.”


So instead you focus on the immediate goal right in front of you. Execute this one, and this step takes care of the next step, and that one takes care of the next, and you just keep going in the direction of the ultimate goal. You embrace each little win, each little win, each little win, until you get there.


I’ll be honest, there are times you’re impatient and you just want to get to the point. But I’ve been around long enough now to really understand it’s about the journey. Some of the most special days were packing into the car with my friends, eating fast food, skating random alleyways in downtown LA, dreaming about being where I’m at now. Staying present and enjoying that is the actual reward.


Rodriguez credits the fearless mindset he built through skateboarding as the foundation for how he runs his business. *Primitive Skateboarding*


### On being called a sellout—and redefining the word:


When I first signed to Nike, a lot of the industry called me a sellout and gave me grief. Skateboarding is very counterculture, very rebellious—this is our world, everybody stay out. But that’s not what drew me to skating. What drew me in was the physical act of it: How can a human being be capable of these amazing feats?


Growing up watching my dad live his dream as a comedian at the highest level, I associated living your dream with making a good living. So from the very beginning, when I fell in love with something, I naturally figured I wanted to make a great living doing it, too.


To me, you’re actually more of a sellout doing something you wouldn’t do for free. I skated for years for free—I was getting paid in joy. How many people would go to their job for a day for free? So I was like, There’s no way I’m a sellout. Of course I’m going to get paid, but I love this. This is my dream.


### On why playing it safe makes you invisible:


It’s just a personality trait—I can’t find neutral. If you play safe, then you might as well be invisible. Whether it’s my skating or the brand, I’m always pushing it. Sometimes you push to the point where you get hurt, and sometimes you push your luck the other way and wonder, Am I going too far? Am I losing credibility? Am I losing respect?


With Primitive, that means doing collabs with Dragon Ball Z or hip-hop artists, bringing in a whole fan base that has no clue who I am or who’s on the skate team. They just love the product, which is great. But then I’ve got to balance out the scale—get back to the world I came up in and make sure my foundation in skateboarding is secure. Once that feels solid, I push back out into the mainstream so I don’t lose ground there.


It’s a constant recalibration, back and forth. Honestly, it exhausts me—so I sleep fine at night.


### On the spray-paint accident that created the gold boards:


The gold boards were a complete accident. If I said I planned it all out, that’d be the biggest lie.


I was at the top of my game, and I knew my name on a product moved the needle at retail. So I figured it was time to put my big-boy pants on and make my own boards. I left Plan B, bought a bunch of blank boards from a manufacturer—just wood, looked like this table—and went to Home Depot for spray paint. I grabbed white, black, and gold, for some reason.


I’m spray painting in my backyard, and the white and black wouldn’t dry right. The paint stayed sticky and bubbled, and I knew that wasn’t gonna skate well. But the gold dried perfectly—smooth, matte finish, really clean. So the white and black were out, and I just started skating gold boards.


People on Instagram started commenting, “Oh, that gold board’s cool, you should put those out.” Little by little I realized people were really into it. Then the manufacturer just sent me boards in gold foil one time—they’d seen it on my Instagram and made them for me. That’s when the light bulb went off.

### On why going direct to consumer cracked the code for pro skaters:


My partner, Heath, and I decided to run a test. We started with 500 boards just to feel out whether we could sell that many. I signed and numbered every single one. Then we made seven videos for a seven-day rollout—every day we dropped a new one, and on the seventh day they went live.


The day we launched I was in Argentina on a Nike tour. It went live at midnight, and by 12:02 it was gone. We sold 500 boards in two minutes. I was like, “Oh my God, we just stumbled into a gold mine.”


I didn’t know what to expect, because skateboarding is fickle—make one move that’s different and people say you’re cutting out the skate shops, you’re evil. But it sold out, and I was like, this is the golden formula. I cracked the code for pro skaters.


The code was just direct to consumer. You put up the money yourself, you sell direct, and you get to keep the profits. And the drop model was huge—that was Heath’s idea. Cool shots, slow-mo tricks so the light glimmers off the board, the music, the edit. We spent relatively little money and the return was great.


Hear Paul’s full conversation on *[Shopify Masters](https://www.youtube.com/@shopifymasters)* for why he refused to name the company P-Rod, the business plan Nike made him build before they’d open the shop, and the people who saw something in him early on.
